P1.evidence: The application was named and then not used — 'Okay, so I saw your application. Tell me, what's been going on?' The prospect knows he was read about but nothing was reflected back to make him feel seen, which is the same half-move on every call in this batch. No four-part frame, no expectations set, no 'does that work?'. The open question landed in a good three-part form: 'What's the main thing you're trying to fix with your fitness, nutrition, health?'

P2.evidence: Six clean hits. Work was covered properly, including the travel pattern that turned out to be the central logistical constraint — 'what do you do for work? Is this mostly sedentary?' then 'How often do you travel?' and 'For a whole week?'. The injury sequence was the best in the batch: asked open ('In terms of any injuries or anything that limits your movements?'), then located it ('this instability, where does it appear, in your legs or hips?'), then extended it into current practice ('do you stretch? Do you do mobility work?') and then, crucially, asked why the practice had stopped. Results from current training were tested directly with 'Would you say that right now you're in a kind of phase of plateau?'. Diet was thorough — meal prep contents, processed food, travel behaviour, sweet tooth and cheat meal. Sleep and energy both asked. Age was volunteered ('I'm 42 now') and height and weight came out only because the rep asked whether he needed to lose weight rather than asking for the numbers, so P2a is partial. Actual days trained per week was never asked. The real gap is P2c: health conditions were never asked, and a substantial family history of type 2 diabetes and hypertension across both parents and all siblings arrived unprompted late in the goals phase.

P3.evidence: By a distance the best Phase 3 in this batch and the only one that reached the bottom. The bridge ran clean and early — 'The question is, like, the bigger question is, why? Why do you want to do this at 42?' — and produced the daughter, the second child and quality of life. P3e was then run properly and twice, which nobody else in the batch did: 'when you get to that best shape, like, what's opening up? What becomes possible?' and, when the first answer was the three-pillars-of-life framing, the rep pushed again with 'and when you check that box out, what happens then?' That second push is what surfaced the family illness material. P3f was approached obliquely rather than asked — 'So you're the only one keeping it healthy?' — which gets partial credit for probing impact without using the scripted question. P3g genuinely drove through to legacy and identity, and the rep did real work there rather than accepting the surface: 'maybe showing up and showing your family that it is possible even later at life that you can get in the best shape of your life. And maybe that will show them to do something about their lives', which landed hard enough that the prospect said 'that's a great point... I never looked at it that way.' And P3h, the reflect-back, actually ran and was confirmed. What is missing is the mobility-strength-energy fork as a discrete question, and 'something physical you want to do but can't', which never came.

P4.evidence: The diagnostic end of the phase ran well and the historical end did not. The missing-piece question was asked cleanly — 'What do you think? Like, what's the missing piece that you're still not in this best shape of your life?' — and the prospect named the gap himself in the phase's own terms: 'for sure nutrition, but that's on me... and then the workouts, all I know how to do are swings... I need to get a program dialed in that I can follow and then grow with.' The rep also ran a genuine root-cause probe on the abandoned mobility work, asking simply 'Why did you stop?', which produced the time trade-off. What never ran systematically is 'what have you tried before' and 'what happened with that' as questions; the training history emerged as context rather than as an audit of failed attempts. And P4f, the move that makes the prospect confront why he cannot do it alone, was not attempted — notable because this prospect had already conceded 'it's all on me' and would almost certainly have gone further.

P5.evidence: Skipped again — the sixth consecutive call in this batch with no consequence frame. The material for it was sitting in the open and the rep walked past it: the prospect volunteered that his parents and all his sisters are on medication for type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure, that 'it's really hitting them really hard', and that he is 'not the average American that's, like, type 2 diabetes, right'. That is a two-year picture already half-drawn by the prospect. Nobody asked what happens if nothing changes, whether he is willing to settle for it, why not, or whether he is ready to draw a line. The rep used the family illness to build a role-model frame instead, which is Phase 3 work — good Phase 3 work — deployed in place of Phase 5.

P6.evidence: The only clean commitment check in the batch, and both questions came before any number. The belief question ran close to verbatim: 'just to make sure we're on the same page, if you had the right nutrition, the right training and accountability from Trevor, do you actually feel that you would get to your goals?' — answered 'Yeah. Yeah. I'm pretty excited that, you know, I made the right decision.' Then the go-all-in question: 'last question, if we can figure out all the details, like logistical part, are you fully committed to showing up and doing the work?' — answered 'Yeah. Accountability is a big thing, and that's 100% on me. So I'm definitely going to make that commitment.' Only then did the rep move to the investment. This is what the phase is supposed to look like.

P11.evidence: One of four steps completed. Payment was collected and verified — the financing link was sent in the Zoom chat, the application approved, a card added and the first payment confirmed, with the rep checking his own end ('Now I see it'). Everything after that was abandoned. The Trevor onboarding call was not booked: the prospect was sitting in his car after a workout without the work laptop holding both his schedules, and the rep deferred it to a WhatsApp message and a possible phone call later that morning. The agreement was never mentioned at any point in the call — not sent, not confirmed, not signed. The welcome email, the Skool community link and the onboarding questionnaire were likewise never raised. The phase intent is to complete every step before hanging up, and the call ended with a paid client holding nothing but a WhatsApp number.

objection_plays.detail: No think-about-it. He had followed Trevor for a year and arrived decided — 'I feel like I've done enough, you know, I just, I kind of let stuff come to me.'
No spouse consult raised, despite a wife and a joint house purchase. He referenced wanting to coach his wife later, never to consult her now.

The trigger was explicit and the play was mostly not run. What did run: the rep's opening probe 'Do you need a payment plan?', which functioned as a permission-adjacent question and produced an unusually full unprompted disclosure; and the value isolate, correctly worded and correctly placed, 'just to triple check, like finances aside, does this thing check off all the boxes for you in terms of how it's structured and that you want to move with this?'. What did not run: the entire financial picture as a sequence. Cash on hand, monthly surplus and credit score all arrived because the prospect volunteered them, not because they were asked — and the volunteered-information rule applies to objection plays as much as anywhere. Number of credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available and investments were never touched. The 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place' frame was absent, as was the scripted permission question. The rep went from 'do you need a payment plan' straight to presenting structures, and when those failed on liquidity he reached for third-party credit. Worth recording that the manager identified this exact failure when the team reviewed this call the same day: 'What made you jump right into giving him payment plan options instead of just, like, going still down the route of OpenWallet?'

The most consequential moment on the call and no play was run. The prospect proposed a concrete delay for a concrete reason: 'do I have to put in the 1,200 first before we do the 1-on-1, Trevor? Because if so, I'd probably wait another two weeks to get my next paycheck... So maybe let's look out two to three weeks from now for that.' That is a cashflow-driven timing objection with a two-to-three week horizon and it was resolvable simply by starting in three weeks. None of the timing moves were used — no 'when does it actually become the right time', no cost-of-delay. Instead the rep established the shortfall ('Okay, so you don't have the 1,200 right now?') and removed the delay by introducing a twelve-month consumer credit product. The objection was resolved commercially rather than answered.

No fear or doubt about the method, the coach or the outcome. He argued the case for Trevor himself: 'Trevor's the only one that you can practice what you preach, and so it's hard to listen to a guy about nutrition if he's not following nutrition.'

Script gap, clinical variety, and the same one already logged against the Tyron Giuliani call. The prospect disclosed an untreated knee injury producing measurable instability and muscular imbalance under unilateral load, plus consequent hip restriction. There is no scripted path for this — no screening question, no clearance prompt, no decision rule about when a body is not suitable for the movement library. The rep improvised the only thing available to him, which was to promise bespoke mobility protocols, and then went further and undermined the professional group best placed to assess it: 'There are a lot of PTs that are sometimes working with kettlebells, but from what I saw, what they're doing, it's not so good.' The gap is the script's; the disparagement is the rep's.

notes: Phases 2, 3 and 6 were the strongest work in the batch — a real why, a real reflect-back, and a genuine belief-and-commitment check taken before the number. It fell apart at exactly two points: the open wallet was skipped in favour of offering structures, which the manager flagged the same day, and Phase 11 stopped at the payment, leaving a paid client with no onboarding call, no agreement and no community access.
